__abstract__.text: Preparation history can make the material measured in an autonomous campaign differ from its recorded recipe. We study confirmation of one frozen recipe under independent fresh preparation. A finite-data analysis distinguishes underdetermination without quantitative regularity from sharp response envelopes under a known Lipschitz bound; a mass-balance memory model yields a contraction-based preparation-bias bound and a conditional fixed-final confidence interval; an exchange argument establishes stronger-wash-first ordering for fixed action counts and enumeration minimizes interval width within a restricted equally weighted preparation menu. Reanalysing original organic-photovoltaic measurements finds 10 threshold disagreements among 240 paired formulations at an illustrative absorbance-loss criterion, without establishing carryover causality. A preserved synthetic benchmark of 48,000 policy runs does not demonstrate superiority of an adaptive heuristic over same-model repetition. A separate extension of 62,400 runs with two measured-data-informed response emulators shows the planner improving true-acceptance yield over costly fresh-only measurement by 3.5 and 4.0 percentage points in high-carryover cases but losing 3.0 points to fixed burn-in/tail repetition when washing is ineffective; strong persistent-memory stress produces 12 false acceptances in 200 campaigns for the misspecified adaptive model and finite observed coverage falls below nominal 95% in some controls. Emulator test errors are moderate and its certificates do not certify physical materials. The contribution is a reproducible conditional confirmation framework with explicit efficiency and failure boundaries; platform-specific carryover, response bounds and marginal costs still require experimental validation.
